report.tagline: An American electric car maker that sells cars directly online and keeps improving them with software updates, plus home and grid batteries.
report.simpleSummary: Tesla makes electric cars like the Model 3 and Model Y, and you buy them on its website or app, not from a dealer. The car gets new features over the internet, like a phone. You can pay a monthly fee for Full Self-Driving (Supervised), which drives the car while you watch the road. Tesla also sells big batteries for homes and power companies, and now runs a small driverless taxi service in Austin.

overview.whatItDoes: Tesla designs, builds and sells electric cars, mainly Model Y and Model 3, plus Cybertruck, Semi and the new two-seat Cybercab robotaxi. It sells directly to buyers, runs its own Supercharger network, and sells software like Full Self-Driving. It also sells Powerwall home batteries and Megapack grid batteries.
howItWorks: Buyers configure and order a car on tesla.com or the Tesla app; there are no franchised dealers.
Tesla builds cars in its own factories in California, Texas, Shanghai and Berlin.
Cars get over-the-air updates that add features, fix bugs and improve range.
Owners pay a monthly subscription for FSD (Supervised); in the US Tesla moved FSD to subscription only in 2026.
The Supercharger network lets owners charge on road trips; other brands now plug in too and pay Tesla.
Mobile service vans and service centres handle repairs, booked through the app.
overview.valueProposition: An electric car that costs little to run, gets better with software, and charges easily on a large network, bought without haggling at a dealer.

businessModel.summary: Tesla makes most of its money selling cars at a profit. On top of that it earns from software subscriptions (FSD), charging, service, regulatory credits sold to other carmakers, and energy batteries. Its big bet is that driverless rides and robots will one day earn more than cars.

revenueStreams.detail: Model Y, Model 3, Cybertruck and others; the largest share of the $28 billion quarterly revenue.
FSD subscriptions, 1.74 million active; Premium Connectivity monthly plan.
Megapack and Powerwall; $2.88 billion in Q3 2026.
Supercharging, repairs, insurance, used cars and parts.
Selling emission credits to carmakers that need them; shrinking over time.

businessModel.pricing: US: Model 3 from about $37,000 and Model Y from about $40,000 for Standard trims (2025 launch prices). FSD (Supervised) is a subscription of about $99 a month in the US. India: Model Y launched in 2025 at about ₹60 lakh before taxes and fees.
costDrivers: AI training compute and chips for FSD and robots
Research and development, up sharply in 2026
businessModel.unitEconomics: On a $42,000 Model Y, Tesla keeps about 18% as gross profit, roughly $7,500, after the cost of building it. Sales, R&D and admin then eat most of that, which is why the company operating margin was only 2.6% in Q3 2026. A buyer who adds FSD at about $99 a month adds roughly $1,200 a year at a very high margin, because the software costs almost nothing to send to one more car. Over 5 years, that subscription could add about $6,000, close to the profit on building the car itself.

growth.moat: Tesla's moat is its data and scale: millions of cars sending driving data to train FSD, its own charging network, and low-cost factories. A rival can build a good EV, but matching the fleet data and software stack takes years. The moat is weaker on cars alone, where BYD and other Chinese makers now build cheaper EVs.

competitors.name: BYD
competitors.positioning: Chinese EV giant with cheap, wide range of cars and its own batteries.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Tesla has fewer models but stronger software, FSD and charging; BYD wins on price and outsold Tesla in Europe in 2026.

competitors.name: Waymo
competitors.positioning: Alphabet's driverless taxi service in several US cities.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Waymo uses expensive sensors and is far ahead in paid driverless rides; Tesla bets on cameras and low-cost cars to scale faster.

competitors.name: Volkswagen, Hyundai and Kia EVs
competitors.positioning: Traditional carmakers with EVs sold through dealers.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Tesla sells direct and updates cars over the air; rivals have more dealer reach and model choice.

competitors.name: Xiaomi and other Chinese tech EVs
competitors.positioning: Phone-like smart cars at low prices.
competitors.howThisProductDiffers: Xiaomi's YU7 competes head-on with Model Y in China; Tesla has global brand and network.

pmLessons: A product can keep earning after the sale if software adds value over time, as FSD and updates show.
Owning the customer relationship (direct sales, app) gives you data and margin, but you also own every service complaint.
Price cuts win volume now but can hurt existing customers through lower resale value.
A founder's brand can drive growth and then become a risk.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you increase FSD subscriptions in Europe?
interviewQuestions.hint: Start with regulation (approved in 9 countries), then trial-to-paid conversion, pricing by country, and trust. Define the funnel and metrics.

interviewQuestions.question: Tesla car deliveries are flat. What would you look at first?
interviewQuestions.hint: Split by region and model. Check demand vs supply, price, competition from BYD, brand sentiment. Propose fixes by segment.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the north star metric for Tesla's robotaxi service?
interviewQuestions.hint: Paid rides completed safely per week. Break into fleet size, utilisation, wait time, safety. Name guardrail metrics like crashes per million miles.

interviewQuestions.question: Should Tesla launch a cheaper car for India?
interviewQuestions.hint: Weigh import duties, local factory, price bands, charging infrastructure, and competition from Tata and Mahindra EVs.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a feature that reduces service centre visits.
interviewQuestions.hint: Use car data for remote diagnosis, predictive part ordering, and mobile service. Measure visits avoided and satisfaction.
